r0v: Being Obnoxious: Too Much, Too Loud, Too Often
r1v: Obnoxious behaviour is acting in ways that overwhelm, irritate or disregard others: dominating conversations, loud boasting, crude jokes, ignoring boundaries or needing to be the centre. It usually grows from insecurity, a need to be noticed, low social awareness or habits that were rewarded somewhere.

r34v: Courage is not the absence of fear. It is doing what is right and good while you are still afraid. It grows step by step, through small brave actions, safe support and trust in God.

r183v: Rohan, the life of the party who lost his friends
r184v: Rohan, 26, a sales executive in Mumbai
r185v: Rohan was always the loudest in the room. He told long stories, interrupted people and made jokes at others' expense. At first friends laughed, but slowly they stopped inviting him. When a close friend finally said, "You never let anyone else talk," Rohan was shocked and hurt.
r186v: Rohan grew up as the middle child of five, where the only way to be noticed was to be the loudest. He believed people would forget him if he was quiet. In groups his excitement and nervousness surged, and he stopped noticing others' faces. Underneath was a deep need to be seen and valued.
r187v: At a church retreat he heard Philippians 2:3-4 and realised he had been using people as an audience rather than loving them.
r188v: Asked two friends for honest feedback
r189v: Practised one question for every story
r190v: Did an impact check in conversations
r191v: Let others finish their stories without topping them
r192v: Prayed each morning to receive his worth from God
r193v: Rohan learned that love "vaunteth not itself" (1 Corinthians 13:4) and that he was already seen and valued by God (Psalm 139). Philippians 2:3-4 taught him to look to others' interests. He no longer needed to perform to matter.
r194v: God designed Rohan's energy and humour as gifts. When used to serve rather than to be noticed, they drew people in. Secure in God's love, he could make room for others.
r195v: Philippians 2:4|Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
r199v: It took months, and he still slips when excited. But friends noticed the change and began inviting him again, and he found deeper friendships than before.
r200v: Real connection comes from making room for others, not from being the loudest.
r201v: Rohan talked too much and people stopped inviting him. He learned to ask questions and listen, and his friends came back.
r202v: Priya finds her voice at work
r204v: Priya noticed errors in her team's reports that could cost the company, but she was too afraid to say anything in meetings. She also stayed silent when a colleague was mocked. Each time she went home ashamed and anxious.
r205v: Priya grew up in a home where speaking up meant being scolded. Her amygdala now fired whenever she imagined disagreeing. Avoidance gave relief, but it made her fear grow and her self-respect shrink.
r206v: Her pastor preached on Esther 4:14, and Priya asked God for courage. She decided to start small.
r207v: Built a courage ladder from sending an email to speaking in a meeting
r209v: Asked a supportive colleague to back her up
r210v: Spoke up about the report errors
r212v: Priya held on to Joshua 1:9 and 2 Timothy 1:7. She learned that courage did not mean the fear disappeared, but that God was with her as she acted. Proverbs 31:8 reminded her that speaking up for others is love.
r213v: God designed courage to grow step by step, and He designed community to strengthen us. Each brave step taught Priya's brain that she could cope, and her supportive colleague made it easier.

r219v: Courage grows in small steps, and God is with us while we are still afraid.
r220v: Priya was scared to speak up. She took small brave steps, and now she can say what is right.

r274v: Scripture calls us to look not only to our own interests but also to the interests of others (Philippians 2:4), and to be swift to hear and slow to speak (James 1:19). Love does not behave itself unseemly or seek its own way (1 Corinthians 13:5). Checking how we affect people is an act of humility and love, noticing others as Jesus noticed the overlooked in every crowd.
r275v: Reading faces and adjusting our behaviour uses the brain's social networks, including areas that track others' emotions and monitor our own actions. When we are anxious or excited these networks can go quiet, and we miss signals. Deliberately pausing to check faces and the balance of conversation strengthens them. With practice, social awareness becomes faster and more natural.
r276v: God designed us for relationship, with brains wired to tune into one another. Self-awareness lets love be wise, so that our energy blesses rather than overwhelms. It reflects Christ, who knew when to speak and when to be silent, and who always made room for the other person.
r277v: "A fool hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself" (Proverbs 18:2). Scripture prizes the person who draws out others' hearts (Proverbs 20:5) and esteems others better than themselves (Philippians 2:3). Jesus asked many questions, inviting people to share their thoughts. Asking questions is a practical way to love.
r278v: Conversations where both people take turns create a sense of connection and trust. Research suggests that people who ask more follow-up questions are liked more. Questions also shift attention from self-focus to curiosity, which calms social anxiety and the urge to perform. Over time this habit rewires conversational patterns.
r279v: God designed relationships as a two-way exchange of love. When we ask and listen, we honour others as image-bearers with stories worth hearing. This reflects God, who listens to His people and invites them to speak.
r280v: God told Joshua again and again to be strong and courageous, not because Joshua felt brave, but because God would be with him (Joshua 1:9). Scripture shows courage growing over time: David faced a lion and a bear before Goliath. God strengthens and helps us (Isaiah 41:10). Taking small steps is how faith becomes action.
r281v: When we repeatedly face a feared situation in manageable steps, the amygdala learns that the danger is smaller than it predicted, and fear decreases. This process, called exposure, is one of the most effective ways to reduce fear. Each successful step also builds self-efficacy, the belief that you can cope, which makes the next step easier.
r282v: God designed courage to grow through practice, as muscles grow through use. He meets us at each step rather than demanding giant leaps. This reflects His patient character, training His people over time so they can face larger challenges with Him.
r283v: "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction" (Proverbs 31:8). Esther risked her life to speak, and the early believers prayed for boldness to speak God's word (Acts 4:29). God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind (2 Timothy 1:7). Speaking up is often an act of love and justice.
r284v: Before speaking up, the body releases stress hormones and the voice may shake. This is the normal fear response, not a sign that you should stop. When you speak anyway and survive the discomfort, the brain learns that it can cope. Short, prepared "I" statements reduce the load on the thinking brain, making courage easier.
r285v: God designed our voices to bless, protect and tell the truth. He gives courage through His Spirit, not by removing fear but by strengthening us within it. When we speak with love and courage, we reflect Christ, who spoke truth gently and boldly.
r286v: Love "vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly" (1 Corinthians 13:4-5). Proverbs warns that a man who is wise in his own eyes has less hope than a fool, and invites us to let others praise us (Proverbs 27:2). Yet God does not reject loud or energetic people. He shapes them. Peter was impulsive and outspoken, and Jesus patiently trained him into a humble shepherd.
r287v: Obnoxious behaviour often comes from an anxious need to be noticed or from low awareness of social cues. Excitement or nervousness floods the brain with arousal, and the self-monitoring networks go quiet. Practising pauses, questions and checking faces builds self-awareness. Receiving honest feedback also helps the brain update its picture of how we come across.
r288v: God designed each person with a unique energy and voice, meant to bless others. When we feel secure in His love, we no longer need to grab attention, and our energy can serve rather than overwhelm. This reflects His design for a body where every part has a place and no one needs to crowd out another.
r289v: Scripture is full of afraid people who became courageous: Moses, Gideon, Esther and Peter. God did not wait for them to stop being afraid. He promised His presence: "Be strong and of a good courage... for the LORD thy God is with thee" (Joshua 1:9). Courage in the Bible rests on God's faithfulness, not on our feelings.
r290v: Fear activates the amygdala and the body's alarm. Avoiding what we fear brings relief, but it teaches the brain that the danger was real, so fear grows. Small brave actions do the opposite: they show the brain that we can cope, and fear gradually shrinks. Support from others also calms the stress response and makes courage easier.
r291v: God designed us to grow courage through relationship with Him and with others. He goes before us and stands with us, so we never face fear alone. When we act bravely in His strength, we become more fully the people He made us to be.
